case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the SEC may obtain disgorgement in a civil enforcement action without proving that investors suffered pecuniary harm.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 15 U.S.C. § 78u(d), particularly subsections (d)(3) (civil penalties) and (d)(7) (express authorization of disgorgement, added after Liu), and the equitable-limits framework articulated under the federal courts’ equitable powers as discussed in Liu v. SEC.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Sripetch argues disgorgement is not properly ‘equitable’ unless it is tethered to restoring victims for actual financial loss; therefore, a showing of investor pecuniary harm is a prerequisite. He contends that allowing disgorgement without proof of investor loss turns the remedy into a punitive, indeterminate sanction (functionally a penalty), raising separation-of-powers and due-process concerns because Congress—not the SEC or courts—must clearly define punishments and their limits. He further maintains that post-Liu and post-amendment disputes (e.g., Hallam vs. Govil) confirm the need for a clear rule that prevents disgorgement from exceeding equitable bounds and becoming a free-floating monetary punishment.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The SEC (represented by the Solicitor General and SEC counsel) argues that disgorgement is aimed at depriving wrongdoers of ill-gotten gains and preventing unjust enrichment, not solely compensating investors, and thus does not require a threshold showing that investors experienced pecuniary harm. The Commission’s position is that disgorgement can be appropriate even when victim losses are difficult to quantify or when misconduct produced gains without a directly measurable investor loss, so long as the award reflects net profits causally connected to the violation and fits within the statutory authorization and governing limits.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to insist that equity cannot be a vehicle for punishment, and Liu’s “for victims” language is a real constraint that courts must take seriously to avoid transforming disgorgement into a penalty. But as Justice Alito emphasizes, Congress enacted § 78u(d)(7) after Liu and authorized “disgorgement” without writing an investor-pecuniary-loss element, so judicial minimalism counsels enforcing Liu’s net-profits/causation/victim-oriented guardrails rather than adding a categorical loss prerequisite that the statute does not contain. The narrower, institutionally safer disposition is to hold disgorgement permissible only insofar as it is limited to net profits causally connected to the violation and is directed to investors where feasible, with any punitive objectives left to § 78u(d)(3). That approach answers Thomas’s historical-equity concern case-by-case without destabilizing the post-Liu statutory scheme by importing an atextual threshold requirement.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s point that § 78u(d)(7) “expressly authorizes disgorgement” and does not add an investor-loss element, and I agree we must not write extra conditions into statutes. But Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s proposed solution—relying on Liu’s “guardrails” alone—still permits awards that function as punitive exactions whenever the SEC cannot identify victims to receive the money, because equity’s original public meaning did not include revenue-raising transfers to the Treasury under the label “disgorgement.” Liu is not merely a policy gloss; it is a statement about what counts as equitable restitution, and Congress’s use of “disgorgement” within an “equitable relief” authorization should be read to incorporate that historically rooted limitation rather than to expand equity by implication. Because § 78u(d)(3) already supplies penalties, I would not construe § 78u(d)(7) to authorize a profits-based monetary award untethered to restoring identifiable victims (or their pecuniary harm) without collapsing the statutory distinction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to warn that a profits-based award untethered from restoring victims can morph into a penalty, which Congress addressed separately in § 78u(d)(3). But as the Chief Justice notes, Liu’s way of policing that problem was to impose functional equitable guardrails—net profits, causal connection, individualized liability, and directing funds to investors where feasible—not to announce a categorical prerequisite of provable investor pecuniary loss. The text of § 78u(d)(7), enacted after Liu, authorizes “disgorgement” without an investor-loss element, and under a textualist approach we should not add a limitation Congress did not write; instead, courts should reject awards that become punitive in application. A bright-line pecuniary-harm requirement would also produce serious practical enforcement gaps in cases with clear unjust gains but diffuse or hard-to-quantify investor losses, without any clear statutory command.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to warn that equity cannot be used as a backdoor penalty, and his emphasis on Liu’s victim-orientation usefully polices that boundary; but Liu’s limitation is best enforced through its concrete guardrails—net profits, causal connection, individualized liability, and a genuine effort to return funds—rather than by imposing a categorical investor-pecuniary-loss prerequisite. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, § 78u(d)(7) was enacted after Liu and authorizes “disgorgement” without adding an investor-loss element, so reading one in would be an atextual narrowing that would predictably undercut enforcement where harm is real but diffuse and hardest on vulnerable investors. Thomas’s penalty concern is addressed case-by-case by rejecting awards that exceed net profits or are not structured for victims where feasible, while leaving truly punitive objectives to § 78u(d)(3) penalties. Under my pragmatic approach, preserving a tightly cabined disgorgement remedy better protects market integrity and access to justice without letting disgorgement drift into punishment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s central point—that equity historically targets restoration for victims and that untethered profit-stripping can look punitive—squarely raises the line-drawing problem, but it does not overcome the enacted text: § 78u(d)(7) authorizes “disgorgement” without an investor-pecuniary-loss element while § 78u(d)(3) separately provides penalties. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize, Liu’s “for victims” language is best read as a limiting principle to keep disgorgement nonpunitive (net profits, causation, individualized accounting, and return where feasible), not as a categorical prerequisite of provable out-of-pocket loss in every case. Under a pragmatic textualist approach, importing a bright-line loss requirement would add an atextual condition and create administrability problems in cases with diffuse or hard-to-quantify harms, whereas enforcing Liu’s guardrails case-by-case preserves statutory coherence between disgorgement and penalties. Thomas’s concern is addressed not by rewriting § 78u(d)(7), but by refusing awards that exceed net profits or operate punitively in function.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to warn that equity historically aims at restoring victims and that an untethered monetary exaction can masquerade as a penalty, which Congress separately authorized in § 78u(d)(3). But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize, § 78u(d)(7) expressly authorizes “disgorgement” without a textual pecuniary-harm element, and reading one in would add a limitation Congress did not enact and risk converting disgorgement into a compensatory-damages regime. Liu’s “for victims” language is best enforced as a guardrail—net profits, causal connection, individualized accounting, and distribution where feasible—rather than as a categorical prerequisite of provable investor out-of-pocket loss in every case. If an award would function punitively or lack a sufficient causal tether to net profits, courts can and should reject it under Liu and the statutory separation between disgorgement and penalties.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press the historical equity point that a profits remedy untethered to victims can drift into a penalty, and Liu’s “awarded for victims” language is the best textual support for that concern. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize, Congress’s post-Liu enactment of § 78u(d)(7) authorizes “disgorgement” without an investor-pecuniary-harm element, and institutional minimalism counsels against adding a categorical prerequisite that the statute’s text does not contain and that would be unworkable where harms are diffuse or hard to quantify. Under my methodology, the proper way to honor equity’s limits is to enforce Liu’s guardrails—net profits, causation, individualized liability, and returning funds to investors where feasible—while treating truly punitive exactions as § 78u(d)(3) penalties. Thomas’s approach would effectively rewrite § 78u(d)(7) into a compensatory-loss requirement that Congress did not adopt, risking needless disruption of a now-codified remedial scheme.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press the historical point that equity’s monetary remedies should not become punitive, and Liu’s repeated references to awards “for victims” underscore that concern. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize, Liu operationalized that limit through guardrails—net-profits accounting, causal connection, and distribution to investors where feasible—rather than by announcing a categorical requirement that the SEC prove measurable investor pecuniary loss in every case. Textually, § 78u(d)(7) authorizes “disgorgement” without an express loss element, and adding one would be an atextual narrowing inconsistent with an original-public-meaning approach that gives effect to Congress’s chosen term, while still policing penalty-like features through Liu and the separate civil-penalty provision in § 78u(d)(3). On that framework, Thomas’s penalty concern is addressed case-by-case by ensuring the award tracks net profits and is not administered as punishment, not by rewriting the statute to impose a universal investor-loss prerequisite.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that equity historically targets restoring victims and that Liu’s “awarded for victims” language reflects that tradition—deserves weight, but it does not justify converting Liu’s anti-punitiveness guardrail into a categorical pecuniary-loss element that Congress did not write into § 78u(d)(7). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 78u(d)(7) expressly authorizes “disgorgement” without an investor-loss prerequisite, and atextually importing one would unduly disable the remedy in cases where unjust gains are concrete but victim losses are diffuse or difficult to quantify. Procedural fairness is better served by rigorous application of Liu’s limits—net profits, causal connection, individualized accounting, and returning funds to investors where feasible—while treating amounts that function as punishment as penalties under § 78u(d)(3). Under that pragmatic, consequence-sensitive approach, Thomas’s penalty concern is addressed through careful tailoring rather than an administratively brittle threshold rule.

John Roberts.reasoning: Liu v. SEC permits disgorgement as an equitable remedy when it is limited to the wrongdoer’s net profits, is causally connected to the violation, and is awarded for the benefit of investors; it did not adopt a categorical prerequisite that the SEC prove investors suffered pecuniary harm in every case. Congress’s post-Liu enactment of 15 U.S.C. § 78u(d)(7) expressly authorizes disgorgement, and a narrow reading that adds an extra-textual “pecuniary-harm” element risks destabilizing settled enforcement practice and inviting broader institutional disruption. Consistent with institutional legitimacy and minimalism, the better course is to hold the SEC may seek disgorgement without proving investor loss so long as courts rigorously apply Liu’s equitable limits (net profits, no joint-and-several absent partnership, and disposition for investors where feasible) and use § 78u(d)(3) penalties—not disgorgement—when the award would become punitive. That approach preserves precedent, respects the statutory scheme, and keeps the remedy within equitable bounds without announcing an overbroad rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under the traditional public meaning of “equitable relief,” a profits-based remedy must be tethered to restoring the status quo for persons wronged by the violation; otherwise it operates as a punitive exaction better characterized as a “penalty,” which Congress separately addressed in 15 U.S.C. § 78u(d)(3). Liu v. SEC held that any SEC “disgorgement” permissible as equity must be limited to net profits and generally be “awarded for victims,” signaling that equity does not authorize free-floating monetary sanctions untethered to victim loss. Section 78u(d)(7)’s later use of the label “disgorgement” cannot expand equity beyond those historically recognized limits absent clearer textual direction, particularly given the constitutional concerns that attend agency-driven punishment. Because the SEC seeks disgorgement without demonstrating investor pecuniary harm, the remedy departs from equitable restitution and should be disallowed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 78u(d)(7), enacted after Liu, expressly authorizes the SEC to seek “disgorgement,” and nothing in that text conditions the remedy on a threshold showing that investors suffered pecuniary harm; importing such a prerequisite would add a limitation Congress did not write. Liu v. SEC held only that any disgorgement awarded as equitable relief must conform to traditional limits—tethered to the defendant’s net profits and causally connected to the violation, with attention to returning funds to victims where feasible—rather than functioning as an open-ended penalty. Requiring proof of investor loss in every case would unduly hamstring enforcement in situations where gains are clear but losses are diffuse or hard to quantify, and it would conflict with disgorgement’s core unjust-enrichment function. So long as courts ensure the award reflects net profits and respects Liu’s equitable constraints (and does not duplicate civil penalties under § 78u(d)(3)), disgorgement may be ordered without proving investor pecuniary harm.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 78u(d)(7)’s express post-Liu authorization of “disgorgement” is best read to permit the SEC to strip net profits causally connected to a securities-law violation without imposing a categorical prerequisite that investors prove (or the SEC identify) measurable pecuniary loss in every case. Liu v. SEC permits disgorgement as equitable relief when it is limited to a wrongdoer’s net profits, tied to the misconduct, and oriented toward victims where feasible—limits that constrain punishment without converting disgorgement into a free-floating penalty. Requiring a threshold showing of investor pecuniary harm would unduly narrow Congress’s remedial scheme and risk leaving vulnerable or diffuse victim groups without effective redress where losses are hard to quantify, while net-profits disgorgement still prevents unjust enrichment and deters fraud. Any due-process or separation-of-powers concern is addressed by enforcing Liu’s equitable guardrails (net profits, no joint-and-several absent partnership-like facts, and a realistic effort to return funds) rather than by adopting an inflexible pecuniary-loss requirement not found in § 78u(d)(7).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 78u(d)(7) expressly authorizes “disgorgement,” and nothing in that text makes a threshold showing of investor pecuniary harm a prerequisite; reading such a requirement into the statute would import a limitation Congress did not adopt, while § 78u(d)(3) separately governs punitive “civil penalties.” Liu v. SEC cabined equitable disgorgement to net profits causally connected to the violation and emphasized returning funds to victims “where feasible,” but it did not hold that investor out-of-pocket loss is always necessary to justify depriving a wrongdoer of unjust enrichment. A workably administrable rule is that the SEC must prove net profits and traceability/causation, with courts ensuring the award is not punitive (no joint-and-several overreach, no failure to deduct legitimate expenses) and directing distribution to investors when practicable. That approach respects Liu’s equitable limits while giving effect to Congress’s post-Liu choice to codify disgorgement in § 78u(d)(7) without adding an investor-loss element.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 78u(d)(7) now expressly authorizes “disgorgement,” and nothing in its text makes investor pecuniary harm a prerequisite; where Congress speaks clearly, our job is to follow that instruction rather than engraft extra conditions. Liu v. SEC recognized that equity long permitted stripping a wrongdoer’s net profits and warned against turning disgorgement into a penalty by requiring limits such as net-profits calculation and a causal connection to the violation, but it did not hold that proof of investor loss is always required. Reading “disgorgement” to categorically demand a showing of investor pecuniary harm would risk collapsing the statute into a compensatory-loss regime Congress did not enact and would unduly constrain an expressly authorized remedy. The proper separation-of-powers guardrail is to enforce Liu’s equitable limits (net profits, individualized liability, and avoiding punitive character), not to add an atextual harm element to § 78u(d)(7).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 78u(d)(7) now expressly authorizes “disgorgement,” and nothing in its text makes proof of investor pecuniary harm a categorical prerequisite; reading such a requirement into the statute would be judicially created and potentially unworkable in cases where gains are clear but losses are diffuse or hard to trace. Liu v. SEC permits disgorgement as equitable relief so long as it is limited to the wrongdoer’s net profits, is causally connected to the violation, and is structured consistently with traditional equity limits to avoid becoming a penalty—constraints that can be enforced without demanding proof of investor loss in every case. The better institutional course is to apply Liu’s guardrails (net profits, individualized liability, and attention to returning funds to victims where feasible) rather than adopt a bright-line rule that could disable a congressionally authorized remedy. If in a particular case the award functions punitively—e.g., exceeds net profits or is untethered from equitable principles—that concern can be addressed under Liu’s penalty-avoidance framework and the separate civil-penalties provision in § 78u(d)(3).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 78u(d)(7) expressly authorizes "disgorgement" in SEC civil actions, and the ordinary meaning of that term—especially against the backdrop of equity—centers on stripping a wrongdoer’s net profits, not on a threshold showing that victims suffered pecuniary loss. Liu v. SEC allows disgorgement only within equitable limits (net profits, causal connection to the violation, and awards structured "for the benefit of investors"), but it did not hold that investor out-of-pocket loss is a prerequisite in every case; rather, it required that the remedy not become punitive. Reading § 78u(d)(7) to impose a categorical pecuniary-harm requirement would add atextual conditions and could defeat Congress’s choice to authorize disgorgement even where harms are difficult to quantify, so long as Liu’s constraints prevent the award from operating as a penalty. Precedent and methodological consistency are satisfied by adhering to Liu’s net-profits and nonpunitive framework, not by engrafting an additional injury requirement absent from the statutory text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 78u(d)(7) now expressly authorizes “disgorgement,” and reading that authorization to categorically require proof of investor pecuniary harm would unduly narrow Congress’s chosen tool and risk under-enforcement where gains are clear but losses are diffuse or hard to quantify. Liu v. SEC constrains disgorgement by requiring a causal link to the violation and limiting the award to a wrongdoer’s net profits, with attention to returning funds to harmed investors where feasible, but it did not adopt a threshold rule that disgorgement is unavailable absent a showing of investor loss in every case. Procedural fairness and due process concerns are addressed by enforcing Liu’s equitable limits (net profits, no punitive add-ons, individualized accounting) and by policing distribution plans, rather than by imposing a rigid pecuniary-harm prerequisite. As a practical matter, allowing disgorgement to strip unjust enrichment—subject to Liu’s guardrails and the statutory framework in § 78u(d)—better protects market integrity without converting disgorgement into an indeterminate penalty.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the SEC may obtain disgorgement in a civil enforcement action without proving that investors suffered pecuniary harm (i.e., that victims were financially worse off).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Exchange Act, 15 U.S.C. § 78u(d), particularly subsections authorizing monetary remedies including § 78u(d)(3) (civil penalties) and § 78u(d)(7) (disgorgement), as informed by limits on equitable relief discussed in Supreme Court precedent.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Sripetch argues disgorgement is permissible only as a victim-centered, equitable remedy (not a punishment), so the SEC must show investors suffered pecuniary harm; otherwise, disgorgement becomes an indeterminate penalty that exceeds equitable authority, raises separation-of-powers and due-process concerns, and conflicts with the restitutionary principles emphasized in Liu (net profits, awarded for victims). Petitioner also relies on the emerging circuit split (e.g., Second Circuit) to contend the Ninth Circuit wrongly allowed disgorgement without a concrete showing of investor loss.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The SEC argues that disgorgement’s core function is to strip wrongdoers of ill-gotten gains to prevent unjust enrichment and deter violations, and that requiring a showing of investor pecuniary harm is not a prerequisite—many securities-law violations generate wrongful gains even when investors cannot be shown to be financially worse off or when harm is diffuse or hard to quantify. The SEC maintains that modern statutory authorization for disgorgement in § 78u(d) permits disgorgement in SEC civil actions subject to established constraints (e.g., causation and net profits), and that the Ninth Circuit correctly upheld disgorgement without imposing an additional, categorical pecuniary-loss requirement.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas presses the best point for Petitioner: Liu’s phrase that disgorgement be “awarded for victims,” coupled with Kokesh’s warning about punitive SEC disgorgement, counsels against allowing the Commission to use disgorgement as a revenue-raising sanction untethered to harm. But I agree with Justice Kagan that Liu is better read as supplying equitable guardrails—net profits, causal nexus, and victim-oriented distribution where feasible—rather than silently adding a categorical, threshold requirement that the SEC prove investor pecuniary loss in every case, which § 78u(d)(7) does not textually impose. Under a minimalist approach, the narrower and more institutionally stable course is to affirm while emphasizing that disgorgement must remain restitutionary in operation (no deterrence-only or punitive awards, no exceeding net profits, and an effort to return funds to harmed investors when practicable), leaving case-specific applications to lower courts. Kokesh heightens the need for those constraints, but it does not justify rewriting “disgorgement” into a loss-based damages element Congress did not enact.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that § 78u(d)(7) contains no express “pecuniary harm” element and that Liu spoke in terms of equitable “guardrails” rather than a rigid evidentiary checklist. But the textual question is what Congress incorporated by using the term “disgorgement,” and Liu identifies the equitable meaning that keeps disgorgement remedial rather than punitive—net profits and an award “for victims”—a limitation that is not satisfied by unjust enrichment in the abstract when there is no demonstrated investor financial setback to which the award can be directed. Without some showing of victim pecuniary harm, “for victims” becomes a formalism and risks converting § 78u(d)(7) into an open-ended monetary sanction that collapses into (and evades the constraints on) § 78u(d)(3) civil penalties, the very penalty concern flagged in Kokesh. Justice Alito’s worry about diffuse harms goes to administrability, not meaning; equity’s remedial power was not a license to impose revenue-raising exactions untethered to making injured parties whole.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s argument—that Liu’s phrase “awarded for victims” necessarily presupposes proof of investor pecuniary harm—is the most serious challenge because it tries to keep disgorgement from drifting into a penalty under Kokesh and from duplicating § 78u(d)(3) civil penalties. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, neither § 78u(d)(7)’s text nor Liu’s holding establishes a categorical, threshold loss element; Liu instead polices the remedy’s equitable character through net-profits limits, a causal tether to wrongdoing, and a victim-oriented disposition “where feasible.” Reading “disgorgement” to require proof that identifiable investors are financially worse off in every case would, as a practical matter, immunize profitable misconduct whenever losses are diffuse or hard to quantify, and that kind of atextual overlay is not restrained textualism. The better course is rigorous enforcement of Liu’s guardrails to prevent punitive, deterrence-only awards while preserving Congress’s authorization of disgorgement as a gain-based equitable remedy.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Liu’s phrase “awarded for victims” could be read to presuppose proof of investor pecuniary harm, to prevent disgorgement from becoming a penalty under Kokesh. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, neither § 78u(d)(7)’s text nor Liu’s holding creates a categorical threshold element requiring the SEC to prove investors were financially worse off in every case; Liu instead cabins the remedy through net-profits limits, a causal nexus, and victim-oriented distribution where feasible. Making pecuniary loss a universal prerequisite would be a judicially created barrier that, in practice, would most often defeat relief where wrongdoing yields clear illicit gains but harms are diffuse or hard to monetize—exactly the settings where vulnerable investors most need effective enforcement. The better way to honor Kokesh and the statute’s structure (including separate civil penalties) is to rigorously enforce Liu’s equitable guardrails to prevent punitive drift, not to graft on an atextual loss element.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press that Liu’s “awarded for victims” language and Kokesh’s penalty warning mean we must police disgorgement so it does not become a de facto fine, especially given § 78u(d)(3)’s separate civil-penalty scheme. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that neither § 78u(d)(7)’s text nor Liu’s holding supports engrafting a categorical, threshold requirement that the SEC prove investor pecuniary loss in every case; Liu’s point was to confine the remedy’s form—net profits, causal tether, and victim-oriented distribution where feasible—so it remains equitable rather than punitive. Treating “for victims” as a universal loss element would be atextual and unworkable in common cases where unjust gains are concrete but harm is diffuse or not readily monetized, effectively letting wrongdoers keep ill-gotten profits. The proper middle course is rigorous application of Liu’s guardrails and careful avoidance of duplicative punishment, not a new prerequisite Congress did not write.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to insist that “disgorgement” in § 78u(d)(7) carries an equitable meaning and cannot be allowed to morph into a punitive exaction that would sidestep § 78u(d)(3) penalties and Kokesh’s warning. But I do not read Liu’s “awarded for victims” language to impose a categorical threshold element requiring proof of investor pecuniary loss in every case; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Liu is better understood as supplying limiting principles—net profits, a causal tether to the violation, and victim-oriented distribution where feasible—to keep the remedy within equity’s traditional bounds. Textually, engrafting an across-the-board “pecuniary harm” prerequisite onto an unqualified statutory authorization of “disgorgement” would be an atextual rewrite, and it would risk letting defendants retain illicit gains whenever losses are diffuse or hard to quantify, even though equity has long targeted unjust enrichment. The proper course is to enforce Liu’s guardrails strictly in application (including rejecting awards untethered to victims when distribution is feasible), not to add a universal loss element Congress did not write.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press that Liu’s requirement that disgorgement be “awarded for victims,” in light of Kokesh, guards against converting disgorgement into an end-run punitive sanction; that is the central risk here. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts (and Justice Kagan) that Liu is best read as imposing structural equitable constraints—net profits, a causal tether, and victim-oriented distribution where feasible—rather than as creating a categorical threshold element that the SEC must prove investor pecuniary loss in every case. Textually, § 78u(d)(7) authorizes “disgorgement” without adding a loss requirement, and institutionally I am reluctant to graft on an atextual, rigid prerequisite that could disable relief where unlawful gains are clear but losses are diffuse or difficult to monetize. The proper way to respect Liu and avoid punitive drift is to police net-profits and distribution/offset issues rigorously and ensure disgorgement does not duplicate § 78u(d)(3) penalties, not to impose an across-the-board pecuniary-harm proof requirement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press the Kokesh concern that disgorgement can drift into a penalty and that Liu’s phrase “awarded for victims” has compensatory overtones, but that does not justify converting “disgorgement” in § 78u(d)(7) into a categorical, loss-proof requirement Congress did not write. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Liu’s holding operates as a set of equitable limiting principles—net-profits calculation, a causal tether to the violation, and victim-oriented distribution where feasible—rather than a new threshold element requiring proof that identifiable investors are financially worse off in every case. Textually and historically, disgorgement targets the defendant’s unjust gains, and insisting on universal pecuniary-loss proof would risk insulating profitable wrongdoing whenever downstream harm is diffuse or hard to monetize, even though Liu already supplies tools to prevent punitive, revenue-raising awards. I therefore would affirm on the understanding that courts must rigorously enforce Liu’s guardrails to keep awards restitutionary and nonpunitive, without engrafting an extra statutory prerequisite.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to warn that, after Kokesh, untethered disgorgement risks becoming a punitive exaction that would collapse into § 78u(d)(3)’s civil-penalties regime; his “awarded for victims” point usefully underscores the need for real limiting principles. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Liu is best read as imposing constraints on the remedy’s form—net-profits, causation, and victim-oriented disposition where feasible—rather than creating an across-the-board evidentiary prerequisite that the SEC prove individualized investor pecuniary loss in every case. A categorical pecuniary-harm requirement is both atextual in § 78u(d)(7) and practically unworkable in cases with diffuse or hard-to-quantify losses, effectively permitting profitable wrongdoing to be retained. Procedural fairness is better served by rigorous policing against punitive drift under Liu’s guardrails (including rejecting deterrence-only, revenue-raising awards) than by adding a threshold element Congress did not write.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 78u(d)(7) expressly authorizes “disgorgement” in SEC civil actions, and nothing in the text makes investor pecuniary loss a categorical prerequisite; imposing that additional element would be a broad judicial gloss inconsistent with restrained decisionmaking. Liu v. SEC held disgorgement is permissible equitable relief when limited to a wrongdoer’s net profits and awarded for victims, but it did not require the SEC to prove that identifiable investors were financially worse off in every case—disgorgement traditionally targets unjust enrichment even when victim loss is difficult to quantify. A narrow ruling preserving Liu’s constraints (net profits, causal nexus, and directing funds to harmed investors where feasible) protects against turning disgorgement into a penalty (Kokesh) while avoiding a sweeping pecuniary-harm rule that could unduly impair enforcement and destabilize settled practice. The Ninth Circuit therefore may permit disgorgement without a categorical showing of investor pecuniary harm so long as the award remains within Liu’s equitable limits and does not function as punitive deterrence untethered to net profits.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text and structure of 15 U.S.C. § 78u(d) distinguish punitive "civil penalties" in § 78u(d)(3) from equitable remedies, and § 78u(d)(7)'s authorization of "disgorgement" must be read in light of the traditional equitable limits this Court recognized in Liu v. SEC. Liu held that to remain equitable rather than punitive, disgorgement must be limited to the wrongdoer’s net profits and "awarded for victims" as "fair compensation to the person wronged," which presupposes a showing of pecuniary harm to investors. Allowing the SEC to obtain disgorgement without proving investors were financially worse off untethers the remedy from equity and risks converting it into an indeterminate penalty—precisely what Liu (and the penalty analysis in Kokesh) cautioned against—thereby expanding federal power beyond the statutory and constitutional limits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 78u(d)(7) expressly authorizes “disgorgement” in SEC actions, and nothing in its text conditions that remedy on proof that identifiable investors suffered pecuniary loss; reading in such a categorical requirement would add a limitation Congress did not enact. Liu v. SEC permits disgorgement so long as it is constrained to net profits and administered consistent with equitable principles, but it did not hold that the SEC must prove investors were financially worse off in every case—particularly where the wrong consists of unlawful gains that may be difficult to trace to discrete losses. Requiring a pecuniary-harm showing would, as a practical matter, undercut enforcement by allowing violators to retain ill-gotten gains whenever victim loss is diffuse or hard to quantify, contrary to the deterrent and remedial structure reflected in § 78u(d)’s menu of monetary remedies. The better reading is that the SEC must show unjust enrichment and net profits (and comply with Liu’s limits), not prove investor out-of-pocket loss as an additional element.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 78u(d)(7) expressly authorizes “disgorgement” in SEC civil actions, and nothing in that text makes investor pecuniary loss a categorical prerequisite; reading in such a requirement would undercut enforcement where harm is diffuse or hard to quantify and would leave wrongdoers unjustly enriched. Liu v. SEC permits disgorgement so long as it remains tethered to equity’s limits—limited to the wrongdoer’s net profits and causally connected to the violation, and ordinarily directed toward victims rather than functioning as a punitive exaction. Those guardrails address the due-process and penalty concerns Sripetch raises without creating an access-to-justice barrier that would disproportionately harm vulnerable investors in markets where individualized loss proof is often impracticable. Elena Kagan.reasoning: Nothing in Exchange Act § 78u(d)(7)’s authorization of “disgorgement” textually imposes a categorical prerequisite that the SEC prove investors were pecuniarily worse off; the natural focus of disgorgement is the defendant’s unjust gain, not the victim’s provable loss. Liu v. SEC, 591 U.S. 71 (2020), constrains disgorgement’s form—limiting it to net profits and generally directing it to victims—but it does not convert disgorgement into loss-based compensatory damages, nor require proof of individualized investor harm as a threshold matter. Requiring a universal pecuniary-harm showing would be unworkable in many securities-fraud contexts where gains are clear but harm is diffuse or hard to quantify, and it would collapse disgorgement into a damages remedy Congress separately addressed through civil penalties in § 78u(d)(3). So long as courts enforce Liu’s guardrails (causation, net-profits limitation, and victim-oriented distribution where feasible), disgorgement under § 78u(d)(7) remains a coherent, nonpunitive monetary remedy.

Under Liu v. SEC, the constitutional and equitable limiting principles are (1) causation to the violation, (2) net profits (no joint-and-several beyond equitable bounds), and (3) awards structured “for victims,” but Liu did not impose a categorical prerequisite that the SEC prove investors were financially worse off in every case. Reading § 78u(d)(7) to require proof of investor pecuniary harm would add atextual conditions Congress did not write and could unduly disable the remedy against schemes yielding wrongful gains without neatly quantifiable victim loss. The proper guardrails are Liu’s net-profits/victims limits (and ordinary burdens of proof), not an additional, across-the-board pecuniary-harm element.
